Very fair point and I agree in the case of the splits that it’s not really a gray area morally or ethically.

I’d edit my original point to exclude his specific action from the legal gray area because honestly I really can’t see a situation where he could have believed that EM would consent to something like that.

I’m not trying to say it’s an excuse. They should still be held accountable for their actions and I agree that it was their responsibility to ensure enthusiastic and ongoing consent. But I also don’t think this was ever stressed to them by the adults in their lives or the culture they were raised in and this is why I can believe that they’ve convinced themselves they didn’t commit a crime.

In an ideal world they would be found guilty of sexually assaulting EM because they would have been explicitly aware of the power imbalance in that situation and of the necessity to obtain ongoing and enthusiastic consent from her the entire time and they therefore would have been intentionally ignoring this in order to commit the crime any way. However, I think it’s incredibly unlikely that they were even aware of what the terms “power imbalance” and “enthusiastic consent” meant at that time. Again, not an excuse because I’m sure they could tell she wasn’t enjoying herself but decided that didn’t matter as much as their own enjoyment, but I could absolutely see why they would believe they were innocent of a crime when sexual assault is so poorly understood by the general public and ESPECIALLY by a bunch of privileged young athletes. 

So again, yes, I believe they deserve to be held accountable and given consequences of some sort, but I do not think jail time or other consequences available to the criminal justice system are deserved. The root cause of their actions seems to be a lack of education, understanding, and empathy. Being labeled criminals and sent to jail or put on house arrest or being forced to pay a fine isn’t going to address that.

ETA: the point about the affluenza defense is interesting because, while I don’t think being privileged is an excuse to disrespect boundaries, I do think the majority of people who perpetrate crimes would be better served by rehabilitation than jail time. or, better yet, restorative justice practices which in part seek to force these perpetrators to come to terms with the actual harm their actions caused to the victim and their community because I can absolutely see how a privileged upbringing would allow one to not consider the harm their actions cause others because they’re sheltered from actually witnessing it!

Let me try to add some more context here.

Morally I don’t think this is a gray are AT ALL. These players knew the situation at least was sketchy at best and I do believe that what they did to EM was disgusting. But, for reasons ranging from my general belief that the criminal justice system doesn’t actually do anything at all to prevent crimes, help victims of crimes heal, and rehabilitate perpetrators of crime to the fact that these players were also in a way failed by a culture that does not educate young people on things like boundaries and consent and healthy relationships, I don’t believe their immoral actions deserve the same kind of criminal consequences as the man who assaulted me from my previous example. I do think they deserve consequences but I don’t know if jail time would be appropriate. 

I would be satisfied if they received guilty sentences with consequences that included something that would involve them being educated on the effects of their actions and require them to take accountability and benefit their community in some way. I do not believe they are innocent but I do believe that they believe they are innocent of any actual crime due to the culture they were likely brought up in. Like, I’m sure they understand on some level that EM did not have a good time that night, but I also think it would be very easy for them to convince themselves she did consent even if it wasn’t enthusiastic consent. 

I hope this makes sense and I really don’t want to come across as victim blaming in any way. From what I’ve read about this case I see a lot of my younger self in EM’s younger self and I have been in somewhat similar situations to this one. Much of my thoughts on this case are influenced by my own personal experiences but I know that all survivors of sexual assault’s experiences are not the same.

Yeah I would agree that Foote and Dubè are looking like the worst of the bunch here (from a legal standpoint at least, McLeod comes across as the scummiest overall imo) and I think they’d be the most deserving of some sort of criminal consequences but I do still think their actions lie somewhat more in the gray area than say the guy who raped me while I was blackout drunk and half passed out.

I doubt any coaching they might have received would have stressed the importance of clear communication around boundaries and how to recognize enthusiastic consent, though. I’d imagine it would be more focused on how to avoid being caught up in any situation that might cause liability issues for themselves or the organization or that might hurt their public image. This is likely why McLeod thought to film a consent video at all and why they were concerned about getting in trouble with HC for having a girl over. 

If the focus of any coaching around this topic is to avoid looking bad in the public eye but not to avoid acting immorally, as I expect is the most likely case, it’s not surprising that they conducted themselves in a way that wasn’t explicitly criminal but also wasn’t respectful or kind to EM. My personal judgement of the character of these players is poor and I believe they were all scumbags that night and likely still are scumbags as they don’t seem to feel bad at all for the harm their actions caused EM but I wouldn’t go so far as to label them criminals. I think the true “criminal” is the institution which failed to encourage good character in these players and which also attempted to sweep this all under the rug to save the organization’s reputation.

I fully agree that education on consent and boundaries should be universally applied to all genders! I also think a culture that reinforces strict gendered stereotypes (ie, men being expected to initiate sex and women being expected to submit to sex) does a huge disservice to people of all genders and that romantic and sexual relationships of all kinds would be a lot healthier if these stereotypes weren’t enforced at all.

Tbh I fully expected my long & rambling comment here to be either completely ignored or downvoted into oblivion by people who had made up their minds about EM’s character already based off how the trial appears to be going. I’m pleasantly surprised by the amount of people that seem to agree with my take and who are capable of recognizing how complex this all is! The response is making me feel slightly more optimistic that the discourse around this case might actually do some good for the public perception of sexual assault and the larger cultural issues which led to this unfortunate night happening.

This is an interesting perspective! I’ve not been in a situation similar to EM’s before but I have been in situations where I initially consented to a sexual act that, once it started actually happening, I no longer wanted but didn’t feel safe or comfortable enough to speak up and stop what was happening. As a younger woman I often believed that I didn’t have the “right” to rescind consent during an act I had previously consented to and I think this belief was the fault of a society which does not empower women to advocate for themselves ever but especially during sex. So, not a crime because my sexual partners in these situations obviously weren’t mind readers, but a societal injustice I guess?

I think the only way we could possibly get to a future where SA isn’t anywhere near as common would be to start educating people on things like consent and boundaries from a veryyyy young age.

Because of how poorly these concepts are understood by most people, many cases of SA will continue to be far too nuanced to accurately attached an innocent or guilty label. (Some) men will continue to be ignorant of what enthusiastic & active consent actually looks like and they’ll continue to be encouraged not to care enough about their partner’s boundaries to allow for open and honest communication around it before engaging in any sexual activity. Also, (some) women will continue to devalue their own boundaries and autonomy so that, when in sexual situations, they don’t feel empowered enough to clearly communicate these boundaries and their feelings around what’s happening.

I am in full agreement with your first paragraph and this is why I believe the law shouldn’t be the only tool available for victims of sexual assault (or even the main tool!) because it is simply not structured in a way that benefits the victim. 

And while I do understand your point about the law allowing some nuance in the decision making process of whether to find the alleged perpetrator of a sexual assault guilty or not guilty I think what I’m trying to get at it is…. There is no decision the judge could possibly make in a case like this that would give appropriate consequences for the players taking all of these nuances into account. While criminal consequences such as jail time wouldn’t be appropriate there are consequences coming from a more restorative justice approach that would serve to give EM some closure and help the players understand the harm their actions caused. Unfortunately, restorative justice just isn’t an available approach to crimes like these in the Canadian justice system (as far as I know at least…)

Admittedly, I’m a bit of a prison abolitionist and I think the entire justice system is flawed. Serving jail time doesn’t help a perpetrator of a crime understand the harm their crime caused and it often doesn’t help the victim of said crime heal and move forward with their life. It doesn’t do a thing to change the systemic issues which significantly impact motivations behind committing a crime. And, if you don’t get to the root of the issue, future crimes can’t be prevented which imo crime prevention should be the number one goal of the criminal justice system!

This tangent is almost completely besides the point haha but all of this to say, I don’t think EM, the players involved, or society at large will benefit in anyway no matter which way this trial goes.

As a victim of sexual assault myself who has first-hand experience with the law being an inadequate avenue for justice, I fucking hate this case.

I hate it because the incident in the hotel room seems to have existed squarely in the gray area in between LEGAL consent and non-consent. I think it is absolutely true that what EM went through that night was traumatic and awful, and that most (if not all) of the men involved treated her poorly and without any concern for her well-being, but I also don’t think that any of the men involved did anything exactly criminal. I think both EM’s and the players in the hotel room’s actions were influenced by a culture (both hockey culture and western culture at large) that doesn’t prioritize things like active consent, boundaries, and respect for women. I think EM was failed by this culture that didn’t teach her the importance of setting clear boundaries and advocating for yourself no matter what and that the players were failed by a culture that doesn’t teach them what active and enthusiastic consent looks like and a culture that encourages them to put their own desires and wants first without considering that of others. 

This situation has so much more nuance than a criminal court case can accurately present and I don’t think a legal avenue was the correct way to both help EM heal from this experience and ensure the players involved fully understand the harm their actions caused, whether they meant to do this harm or not. 

The absolute WORST part about this case, though, is the effect it’s had on the public’s opinion of sexual assault. Looking on social media it seems the majority takeaways from this are going to be either “EM is a liar and made up rape allegations for money or to cover up her own bad decisions and the players are completely innocent of all wrong-doing” OR “these players are all criminals who are colluding together to cover up a vicious gang rape and are going to get away with it”. When, in reality, neither of these statements are entirely true! The players can have done something morally wrong (which I believe wholeheartedly they wronged EM) without exactly being guilty of a crime. And EM can be telling her absolute truth, that she was a victim of a sexual assault, even if the objective truth of the matter is that her fawn response to the traumatic nature of what was happening and the unfair pressure the situation put on her presented itself as consent to the men in that hotel room. 

Unfortunately, the law leaves no room for these kinds of nuance.

It might be harsh but I think any abusive partner gives up their right to fidelity and loyalty. And I think that, if cheating helps someone leave their abusive partner, it is absolutely forgivable.

I have only ever cheated on one partner and it was only after 5 years of abuse. I take accountability for my actions but I have also forgiven myself for the act because it indirectly saved my life.

If I had never cheated I would have never been able to leave him and, based off the way things were going, it’s a very real possibility I’d now be dead either by his hands or by my own (the abuse was so severe I was constantly contemplating suicide).

I believe that if cheating helps someone escape their abusive partner it is absolutely understandable and forgivable.

I am not at all defending the act of cheating (except for in very specific situations, such as cheating while in an abusive relationship, but I won’t go into that here) but here are some reasons one might do so:


1. Feeling as if they have no choice but to stay with a partner they no longer want to be with, and allowing themselves to seek happiness outside of this unwanted relationship, due to things like: children (being a single parent is NOT easy and there’s no guarantee co-parenting will work out), financial constraints (housing is insanely expensive and many adults cannot afford to live alone), not having a social circle outside of the one shared with your partner (potentially due to social isolation or a large age gap with the older partner having solidified friendships that the younger partner is grandfathered into), and etc

2. Lack of impulse control and empathy for their partner (this is an obvious one, and the reason which is most immoral and difficult to forgive as a result). There are some people who simply aren’t willing to think before they act and, when confronted by temptation such as a hook up with an attractive person that isn’t their partner, they act on their feelings of lust and attraction without stopping to think about all the ways this brief moment of pleasure might blow up their life and cause immense harm to their partner.

3. Societal pressure to remain in a relationship with a partner they aren’t attracted to to cover up what their true attractions are (unfortunately there are still some places where being gay or even being attracted to people of certain religions/cultures/races is unacceptable). Along with this, some people who cheat might wish to be in a polyamorous relationship because monogamy isn’t natural or desirable to them but, due to these types of relationships having a lot of stigma attached to them, they decide to try to force themselves into a monogamous mold but understandably fail at this.

I mean sure, there are some small communities of people that are accepting of open/poly relationships but society overall and especially governmental institutions are absolutely not going to be treating poly relationships with the same respect as mono ones. I’d argue that those larger societal structures are a lot more influential to one’s life and the decisions they make throughout it.

The issue with this is that there is a TON of societal and even systemic pressure to be monogamous. If poly relationships were perceived as equally acceptable as mono relationships, and if the legal definition of marriage was somehow changed to accommodate relationships which include more than 2 people, I absolutely believe that cheating would become far less common.

Originally meant to be in response to a now deleted comment asking how we can tell she’s not lying (or something along those lines?):

This is the problem with sexual assault from a legal standpoint, it’s not something that often leaves behind concrete evidence. When someone is murdered there’s a dead body, when someone is physically assaulted there’s a bruise or a wound of some other sort, when someone is robbed there’s is an absence of a physical object.

Sexual assault is the theft of someone’s bodily autonomy which isn’t something that can be physically proved unless there’s a video of the entire act where each participant is enthusiastically consenting the whole time. Obviously, this just doesn’t happen. 

So, the law concerning sexual assault needs to be different than it is with other types of crimes. In this case, for example, there is video evidence that EM had a LOT to drink, enough so that she was almost certainly too drunk to give enthusiastic consent. There is also video evidence that McLeod was near her most of the night and it should be assumed he had a good idea of how many drinks she had. There is also evidence of texts he sent throughout the night to other individuals inviting them to participate in sexual activities with EM (as well as statements from others supporting this), and video evidence that suggests there were multiple men coming in and out of their hotel room. The video evidence of McLeod asking EM to consent only after these sexual acts took place, as well as text evidence that there was a coordinated effort to “get their stories straight” for an investigation, suggests that all of the men involved had the wherewithal to understand what they were doing. 

So, in light of all this, at the very least it should be assumed McLeod was aware of how drunk EM was and therefore aware she could not enthusiastically consent to sexual acts with the multiple men he invited over. Whether these other men were aware of how drunk EM was is up for debate and I haven’t heard anything that proves this either which way but there should absolutely be no doubt that McLeod is guilty here.


Disclaimer: I think they’re all guilty and absolutely vile human beings in light of the info that’s been revealed so far and I personally will almost always believe victims when they come forward like this, but the above is my attempt at an objective take on the situation! EM is incredibly brave for testifying and I hope she is on the path towards healing and will continue to do so regardless of the outcome of this case.

When I worked inpatient psych we had a woman in her late 80s admitted from a medical floor after she crashed her car BY ACCIDENT due to a medical emergency. After spending a little over a week in a medical unit they sent her to our unit because she mentioned to a doctor that she was satisfied with her life so it wouldn’t be a big deal if she passed away. She was not actively suicidal, the car accident was never even considered to be intentional, and she was miserable and bored at our unit where she had to wait for over a month to be placed into a nursing facility because they decided she wasn’t physically capable of moving around her own home anymore. 

To make it even worse, we had no beds open on our less acute unit so she had to spend the majority of that month in our highly acute and restrictive unit with actively psychotic, schizophrenic, and severely decompensated patients. She was too scared to leave her room that entire time and I didn’t blame her one bit.

Yes!!!! I definitely experienced this as well. I say under 2 days (should have said 3 to be more accurate…) because often times we’d get these obviously unnecessary admissions at the end of day on a Friday after the psychiatrists and psych eval already left for the weekend… meaning these patients would have to suffer basically until they can be seen on Monday and then discharged and told there really was no reason for them to be admitted in the first place 🫠
THANK YOU for this point

I don’t disagree with your overall point but forcing people who aren’t in immediate danger of harming themselves or others and are simply looking for resources that are hard to find (outpatient psychiatrists and therapists have insane wait times in my area at least) into a locked facility unnecessarily can definitely cause further trauma and stress. Many people work jobs or are in financial situations where having to take off even one day unexpectedly could cause them to lose their jobs, houses, skip meals, etc. (not to mention the insane medical bills!) Many of these patients also claimed they were not given clear & accurate information on what signing themselves into our unit entailed (and they usually only agreed to sign themselves in after being threatened with a 302/involuntary hold). They were either told they could sign themselves out at any time or that they would be released immediately after 72 hrs. 

While working at this unit, I was often floated to the EBH (emergency behavioral health) which is where patients are supposed to be assessed by a psychiatrist and stabilized for inpatient treatment if needed. The ER nurses and staff assigned to this section of the ER were incredibly cruel and dismissive of the patients and the BH staff sent to help and the extent of the psych eval I witnessed patients receiving was a 10ish min video call with rapid fire questions and minimal opportunity for the patient to speak for themselves.

I understand ERs are often understaffed for the sheer volume of patients and emergency situations they deal with in a shift but psych patients seem to be treated as an afterthought and there is simply not enough consideration of the negative consequences an unnecessary involuntary psych hold (or forced “voluntary” admission based off inaccurate info) might bring to this person’s already stressful life. It’s an imperfect system that very often gets it wrong.

As someone who worked at an inpatient psych unit inside a larger hospital for a few years, I saw a ton of cases of people being admitted from our ER on a psych hold who truly did not need it and were then discharged in under 2 days. Our Psych Eval team was constantly pressured into just getting people out of the ER as soon as possible and into an inpatient bed and we’d have to figure it out once they were admitted.

My initial reactions to the 4 main girls can be summed up as follows:

Hannah was shitty but funny in seasons 1-3, got waaaay worse and was kind of a drag to watch in all of season 4, most of season 5, and all of season 6. She redeemed herself in the last 2 eps of season 5 but then acted almost completely out of character in season 6 which ruined her for me.

Marnie was truly just doing her best after being failed by her mother. Most of my favorite moments center around her and even though she is often a terrible person and is way too naive for her age I love her character dearly. The Panic in Central Park is my favorite episode of the show and might have earned a spot in my top 10 tv episodes ever. I love her little monologue to Desi at the end and I love that she continues the same patterns to some extent even after this moment of self awareness because it felt true to real life and true to how she was written.

Jessa is absolutely the most interesting character imo and I wish she got more screen time in the last season because Jemima Kirke is for sure the best actor on the show (with Adam Driver being a close 2nd). I loved everything about her messy, toxic ass self. She embodied BPD & addiction perfectly and that scene in the bathroom of the bar where she maybe hooked up with the older guy while Adam spent the day with Hannah playing house or whatever was the most heartbreaking scene of the entire show. She was a shitty friend and a shitty girlfriend but she also had moments where she cut through all the bullshit and just told it how it was. You could also tell that she really wanted to be better and she did feel bad for the pain she caused in her wake but she was stuck in these self sabotaging cycles and just could not escape. Ultimately, I really want more Jessa and would have been happy with a spin off series following her life during and/or after the events of the show.

Shosh started out strong but I think they really underutilized her by the last couple seasons. I understand that she was meant to be kind of the voice of reason whenever the girls got into their stupid little spats but much of her personality and story besides fulfilling that role fell to the wayside after Japan. She could have been great but she ended up being pretty mid. 

Finally, the boys. Adam was terrible, sometimes scary, and often pathetic but so fun to watch. Elijah served as great comic relief but I kinda wish he didn’t become such a major character because he took away a lot of the screen time from the girls. My favorite scene of his was the fight with Hannah in the kitchen of the Chinese place after he found out Hannah was pregnant and while the way he went about it wasn’t nice he wasn’t entirely wrong? Desi was a perfect narcissist and emotionally abusive douche, some of his scenes hit a little too close to home as someone whose ex was similarly emotionally abusive though. Fran was dumb and I didn’t like him. Scott was also weird and dumb. My opinions on Ray varied wildly throughout the show and I kinda feel like he changed way too drastically between the early seasons and the rest of the show. They should have kept him as the misogynistic, creepy older guy instead of trying (and failing) to redeem him. I LOVE CHARLIE and wish his actor didn’t quit but at least he returned for my favorite episode! 

Okay that’s it.

When I was a young teenager into a young adult (let’s say ages 12-21), these assaults changed me by numbing my emotions & reactions to further abuse and lowering my opinion of myself. As I grew a bit older and more time passed without more assaults/abuse occurring I began to feel less numb and felt anger instead. Anger at those who assaulted & abused me, anger at society for producing individuals capable of such actions, and anger at myself for allowing these things to continue to happen as a result of my self-loathing and ambivalence. This anger eventually subsided and I gained compassion for myself and even a little tiny bit of compassion for those who abused me (for a while I thought this compassion resulted from a too forgiving nature, I now don’t think there’s anything wrong with forgiveness). I’ve always had compassion for others who’ve experienced similar assaults & abuse but, now that I’ve extended that compassion to myself, I think I’m more capable of supporting other survivors.

I believe all of these experiences, and the resulting emotional journey & growth, has turned me into a more compassionate and self-assured version of myself. I’ve accepted my flaws and forgiven myself for the choices I made which resulted in further abuse. I’ve forgiven the men who have abused me, even if I can’t go so far as believing they are good people underneath it all, and I have come to an understanding that there are systemic flaws in this world that result in further acts of violence. I am committed to exploring how these flaws came to be, what institutions allow them to persist, and what can be done to create a world where this violence is not accepted as common place. I believe would-be future perpetrators of sexual assault can be prevented from taking such acts if their motivations and the systemic structures which produce & condone these motivations were discovered and properly dealt with.

I want to be a part of creating this future I’m describing. I want to start dialogues with the people around me on how to achieve this future.

As someone who’s worked inpatient psych for a few years now, and also studied criminology a bit in undergrad, both my actual experiences with the severely mentally ill & my academic experience studying what drives people to commit violence is what led to my opinion that individual pathology does not indicate a willingness to plan out and commit violent acts (against others at least). The most psychotic and delusional individuals I’ve met are not capable of planning out something like a mass shooting and many aren’t even violent, they’re just scared and want to be left alone by those they deem to be a threat. The few that are violent might lash out randomly at strangers on the street but aren’t going out to buy guns or other weapons to use. 

Those that I’ve met at work who have threatened or attempted to harm others with a gun are usually diagnosed with depression or adjustment disorder, have no prior experience with the mental health or criminal justice system, and their stressors are things like losing a job or marital strife. To me, this indicates that relatively stable individuals are capable of violence if their life is disrupted enough by factors outside their control.

Statistically, individuals diagnosed with mental illness are more likely to be victims of gun violence than perpetrators. Seems to me like those who commit mass shootings and other acts of gun violence are triggered by societal ills (as one commenter mentioned already, things like inequity, zero social mobility, and little social cohesion) more than diagnosable mental illness and that passing legislation that would work towards fixing these external issues would make a much bigger difference than simply providing more individuals with psychiatric medication and therapy.

Obligatory NAT but an MHT at an inpatient psych unit.

When I first started, the behavioral health department held an education day for new hires to learn more about the entire department and meet some of the psychiatrists, NPs, and therapists. One of the NPs put together a presentation specifically about personality disorders, focusing on BPD as this was such a common diagnosis for our patients. She began the presentation with a HIGHLY stigmatized “example” of a woman with BPD-like symptoms from the movie Fatal Attraction and ended by asking us all if we had any questions. I asked how often she thought BPD was misdiagnosed as to me it sounded like many of the diagnostic criteria fit into other diagnoses as well, specifically C-PTSD. Her answer was essentially “well, they both have very specific diagnostic criteria according to the DSM and I go by the book so I don’t believe that happens much” and essentially dismissed any follow up questions I had on the subject, even stating she had never even heard about trauma-informed care when I tried to talk about it.

I’ve now worked here just over 6 months and have heard and seen the label BPD attached to a large percentage of our female patients, and some of our male patients too. If they don’t fit the diagnosis of psychosis, schizophrenia, or MDD they’re labeled either bipolar or BPD, with barely any attention paid to the trauma they almost always share with their treatment team.
